cards.q: For min f(x) over a set S ⊆ ℝⁿ, define (1) a global minimizer, (2) a local minimizer, (3) the “strict” version of each, and (4) say how these notions imply one another.
pts: (1) Global min: f(x) ≥ f(x*) for all x ∈ S.
(2) Local min: there is ε > 0 with f(x*) ≤ f(x) for all x ∈ B(x*, ε) ∩ S.
(3) Strict versions replace ≤ with < for every x ≠ x* (in S, or in the ball).
(4) Strict global ⇒ global ⇒ local, and strict global ⇒ strict local ⇒ local; a strict global minimizer is unique.
cards.pit: Global does not imply strict: for a constant function every point is a global min and none is strict.

cards.q: Let b ∈ ℝⁿ and let B be an n×n matrix, not necessarily symmetric. Give the gradient and Hessian of (1) bᵀx, (2) xᵀBx, and (3) f(x) = ½xᵀAx + bᵀx + c when A is symmetric.
pts: (1) ∇(bᵀx) = b, Hessian 0 (and ∇(xᵀx) = 2x).
(2) ∇(xᵀBx) = (B + Bᵀ)x, Hessian B + Bᵀ.
(3) ∇f = Ax + b, Hessian A.
cards.pit: ∇(xᵀBx) = 2Bx only when B is symmetric — the slide's derivative table drops this condition.

cards.q: State the first-order necessary condition (FONC) for minimizing f over ℝⁿ: what must be assumed about f and about the point x*, and what does it conclude?
pts: f is differentiable at x*.
x* is a local minimizer of the unconstrained problem min over ℝⁿ (an interior point, so every direction is allowed).
Then ∇f(x*) = 0; such a point is called a stationary point.
cards.pit: The converse is false: f = x³ has f′(0) = 0, but 0 is neither a min nor a max.

cards.q: FONC says: if x* is a local minimizer of a differentiable f on ℝⁿ, then ∇f(x*) = 0. Outline a rigorous proof in three steps.
pts: Fix any direction d; for small t > 0, x* + td is in the ball, so f(x* + td) − f(x*) ≥ 0.
Divide by t > 0 (inequality keeps direction) and let t ↓ 0 using the o(t) Taylor remainder: ∇f(x*)ᵀd ≥ 0 for every d.
Choose d = −∇f(x*): −‖∇f(x*)‖² ≥ 0, hence ∇f(x*) = 0.
cards.pit: The slide ends with “∇f(x*)ᵀd = 0 and d ≠ 0, so ∇f(x*) = 0” — false for a single d (g = (1,0), d = (0,1)). The argument must hold for all d.

cards.q: FONC narrows the search to points with ∇f(x) = 0. What does this achieve, and what are its three limitations?
pts: Can: rule out every non-stationary point and reduce the search to solving ∇f(x) = 0 (n equations, n unknowns).
Cannot tell a min from a max: f and −f have the same stationary points.
Cannot rule out saddle points.
May be vacuous: f = x₁ − 2x₂ has no stationary point at all (unbounded below).
cards.pit: Existence is a separate question: eˣ is strictly convex with infimum 0 but has no minimizer and no stationary point.

cards.q: FONC assumes x* is an interior point and f is differentiable there. Explain what goes wrong in (1) minimizing f(x) = x over x ∈ [0, 1], whose minimizer is x* = 0, and (2) f(x) = |x| at x = 0.
pts: (1) x* = 0 is a boundary point, so only feasible directions d ≥ 0 are allowed and the proof only gives ∇f(x*)ᵀd ≥ 0 for those d — here f′(0) = 1 ≠ 0. This “no feasible descent direction” condition is the seed of KKT.
(2) |x| has a strict global min at 0 but is not differentiable there (one-sided derivatives ±1), so FONC's hypothesis fails.
cards.pit: Non-smooth losses such as the hinge loss have the same issue at the kink — the reason subgradients exist.

cards.q: Define a convex set C ⊆ ℝⁿ, list standard examples, and explain how an affine set differs from a general convex set.
pts: C is convex if x, y ∈ C and λ ∈ [0, 1] imply λx + (1 − λ)y ∈ C (the whole segment stays in C).
Examples: ℝⁿ, ∅, half-spaces {aᵀx ≥ β}, balls, affine sets {Ax = b}, the PSD cone.
Affine sets contain the whole line through two points, not just the segment (any λ ∈ ℝ works).
cards.pit: A union of convex sets is not convex in general: [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3] misses the midpoint 1.5.

cards.q: Which operations on sets preserve convexity? Use them to explain why the LP feasible set {x : Ax ≤ b} is convex.
pts: Intersections (of any number of sets), scaling βC and Minkowski sums C₁ + C₂ of convex sets are convex.
Sublevel sets {g ≤ 0} of convex g are convex, so {gᵢ(x) ≤ 0 ∀i, Ax = b} is convex when every gᵢ is.
LP: {Ax ≤ b} is an intersection of half-spaces, hence convex.

cards.q: Define a convex function and a strictly convex function f on a set S. Why must S itself be convex for the definition to make sense?
pts: f(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) for all x, y ∈ S, λ ∈ [0, 1] — the chord lies above the graph.
Strictly convex: strict inequality whenever x ≠ y and λ ∈ (0, 1). f is concave if −f is convex.
The definition evaluates f at λx + (1 − λ)y, so it only makes sense when S is convex.
cards.pit: “Is 1/x convex?” is ill-posed on ℝ∖{0}; on (0, ∞) it is convex.

cards.q: Let f(x) = ½xᵀAx + bᵀx + c with A symmetric. (1) When is f convex, and when strictly convex? (2) What identity proves this without using the Hessian? (3) Apply it to portfolio variance xᵀQx, where Q is a covariance matrix.
pts: (1) f is convex ⇔ A ⪰ 0, and strictly convex ⇔ A ≻ 0.
(2) λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) − f(λx + (1 − λ)y) = ½λ(1 − λ)(x − y)ᵀA(x − y): the gap is ≥ 0 for all x, y exactly when A ⪰ 0 (if vᵀAv < 0, take x − y = v).
(3) xᵀQx = Var(xᵀr) ≥ 0, so a covariance matrix is PSD and portfolio variance is convex; strictly convex iff Q ≻ 0, i.e. no riskless combination of the assets.
cards.pit: Necessity: if vᵀAv < 0 for some v, choose x − y = v and the identity turns negative.

cards.q: Which operations on functions preserve convexity? Give the rules for (1) sums, (2) positive scaling, (3) composition g∘f, and (4) two further rules needed for ML losses such as hinge and logistic.
pts: Sum f₁ + f₂ is convex; strictly convex if at least one term is.
αf with α > 0 keeps (strict) convexity.
Composition g∘f is convex if f is convex and g: ℝ → ℝ is convex and nondecreasing on the range of f.
Also (not on the slides): affine pre-composition g(Ax + b) and pointwise max of convex functions — needed for hinge and logistic losses.
cards.pit: Drop “nondecreasing” and it fails: g(y) = e^{−y}, f = x² gives e^{−x²}, whose second derivative at 0 is −2.

cards.q: State the Hessian test for convexity of f on a set C: (1) the hypotheses on C and on f, (2) the test for convexity, (3) the test for strict convexity.
pts: C is non-empty, open and convex, and f ∈ C²(C).
f is convex on C ⇔ H(x) ⪰ 0 for all x ∈ C.
H(x) ≻ 0 for all x ∈ C ⇒ f strictly convex — but not conversely: x⁴ is strictly convex with f″(0) = 0.
cards.pit: The slide says “strictly convex iff PD”, which is wrong in the ⇒ direction. “Open” matters too: x₁² − x₂² restricted to the line x₂ = 0 is convex although H is indefinite.

cards.q: For a symmetric matrix, how do you check (1) positive definiteness (PD), (2) positive semidefiniteness (PSD), and (3) PSD for a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [b, c]]?
pts: PD: all leading principal minors > 0, or all eigenvalues > 0.
PSD: all principal minors ≥ 0 — not only the leading ones — or all eigenvalues ≥ 0.
cards.pit: Leading minors ≥ 0 does not give PSD: diag(0, −1) has leading minors 0 and 0 but is not PSD.

cards.q: Call min f(x) over S a convex problem when S is a convex set and f is convex on S. (1) State the “local = global” theorem, including the strictly convex case. (2) Outline its proof: which point z do you construct, and how do you finish?
pts: (1) Every local minimizer of a convex problem is global; if f is strictly convex, it is also unique and strict.
(2) For y outside B(x*, ε), take z = λ′x* + (1 − λ′)y with 1 − λ′ = ε/‖y − x*‖, so z ∈ S and on the ball. Then f(x*) ≤ f(z) ≤ λ′f(x*) + (1 − λ′)f(y); divide by 1 − λ′ > 0 to get f(x*) ≤ f(y).
cards.pit: Both convexities are needed: (x − 2)² on S = [−1, 0] ∪ [1, 3] has a local min at 0 that is not global.

cards.q: Let f be differentiable on an open convex set C. (1) State the gradient inequality that characterizes convexity and interpret it geometrically. (2) What does it imply for a point x* with ∇f(x*) = 0?
pts: (1) f convex ⇔ f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) for all x, y ∈ C (strict for y ≠ x ⇔ strictly convex): the tangent plane is a global under-estimator.
(2) Put x = x*: f(y) ≥ f(x*) for all y, so x* is a global minimizer. For differentiable convex f on ℝⁿ, FONC is therefore necessary and sufficient.
cards.pit: On a constrained convex S the right condition is ∇f(x*)ᵀ(y − x*) ≥ 0 for all y ∈ S, not ∇f(x*) = 0.

cards.q: Least squares: X is the data matrix (n samples × d features), y ∈ ℝⁿ the targets, and we choose weights w ∈ ℝᵈ to minimize f(w) = ½‖Xw − y‖². (1) Give ∇f and the Hessian, and explain why f is always convex. (2) When is the minimizer unique, and what is it? (3) What does the optimality condition mean geometrically? (4) What happens when the uniqueness condition fails?
pts: (1) ∇f(w) = Xᵀ(Xw − y) and H = XᵀX. H is PSD because wᵀXᵀXw = ‖Xw‖² ≥ 0, so f is convex for any X.
(2) Unique iff X has full column rank (no redundant features). Then XᵀX ≻ 0, and setting ∇f = 0 (normal equations XᵀXw = Xᵀy) gives w* = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.
(3) ∇f(w*) = 0 means Xᵀr = 0 for the residual r = Xw* − y: the residual is orthogonal to every column of X.

(4) If X is rank-deficient (e.g. one column is a multiple of another), XᵀX is singular: f is still convex, so local = global, but there are infinitely many minimizers. Ridge (XᵀX + γI ≻ 0) restores uniqueness.
cards.pit: The slides say “full row rank” — backwards. A tall regression matrix can never have full row rank; what is needed is full column rank.

cards.q: For a twice-differentiable f, state (1) the second-order necessary condition (SONC) and (2) the second-order sufficient condition (SOSC). (3) Which case can neither of them decide?
pts: (1) SONC: if x̄ is a local min, then ∇f(x̄) = 0 and H(x̄) ⪰ 0.
(2) SOSC: if ∇f(x*) = 0 and H(x*) ≻ 0, then x* is a strict local min — local only, it says nothing global.
(3) H(x*) PSD but singular: undecided — x⁴ has a min at 0, x³ has neither.
cards.pit: x₁² + x₂⁴ and x₁² − x₂⁴ both have H(0) = diag(2, 0), yet one is a strict min and the other a saddle: look along the null direction.

cards.q: What is a saddle point of f, and which second-order test identifies one?
pts: A stationary point that is neither a local min nor a local max: every neighbourhood contains points with larger and with smaller f.
Test: ∇f(x*) = 0 and H(x*) indefinite (it has both a positive and a negative eigenvalue) ⇒ saddle point.
cards.pit: A PSD but singular Hessian can still be a saddle (x₁² − x₂⁴ at 0); indefiniteness is sufficient, not necessary.

cards.q: Find and classify all stationary points of f(x) = x³ − x² − 4x − 6 (local min or local max), and say whether f has a global minimum.
pts: f″ = 6x − 2: at x₊ = (1 + √13)/3, f″ = 2√13 > 0 ⇒ strict local min.
At x₋ = (1 − √13)/3, f″ = −2√13 < 0 ⇒ strict local max.
No global min: f → −∞ as x → −∞.
cards.pit: The slide prints ∇f = 3x² − 2x − 2, which does not match the stationary points it quotes; the correct derivative is 3x² − 2x − 4.
